section.title: Accepting One Another
section.sectionRationale: Paul brings the discussion of the weak and the strong to its climax and its Christ-centered ground. The strong are not merely to endure the weak but to bear with their failings and to please their neighbor for his good, because Christ Himself did not please Himself. Then Paul lifts the whole matter into the sweep of redemption: Christ became a servant to the circumcised to confirm God's promises and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy. A chain of Old Testament quotations shows that Jew and Gentile praising God together was always the plan. The section ends in a benediction of joy, peace, and overflowing hope.
section.thesis: The strong ought to bear with the weak and please their neighbor for his upbuilding, following Christ who did not please Himself; and the whole church, Jew and Gentile, is to welcome one another as Christ welcomed them, so that with one voice they glorify the God of hope who fills them with joy and peace by the power of the Holy Spirit.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the strong bear with the weak because Christ did not please Himself; welcome one another as Christ welcomed you, confirmed by a chain of Scripture that Jew and Gentile would praise God together; and the benediction of the God of hope who fills His people with joy, peace, and overflowing hope.

units.label: Bear with the weak, as Christ did not please Himself
units.note: the Scriptures written for our hope

verses.text: We who are strong ought to {{bastazo|bear with}} the shortcomings of the weak and not to please ourselves.
Each of us should please his neighbor for his good, to {{oikodome|build him up}}.
For even Christ did not please Himself, but as it is written: “The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me.”
For everything that was written in the past was written for our instruction, so that through endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures, we might have hope.
Now may the God who gives endurance and encouragement grant you harmony with one another in Christ Jesus,
so that with one mind and one voice you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.label: Welcome one another as Christ welcomed you
units.note: Christ the servant of Jews and Gentiles

verses.text: Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you, in order to bring glory to God.
For I tell you that Christ has become a servant of the circumcised on behalf of God’s truth, to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs,
so that the Gentiles may {{doxazo|glorify}} God for His mercy. As it is written: “Therefore I will praise You among the Gentiles; I will sing hymns to Your name.”
Again, it says: “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people.”
And again: “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and extol Him, all you peoples.”
And once more, Isaiah says: “The Root of Jesse will appear, One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles; in Him the Gentiles will put their hope.”

units.label: The God of hope fill you with joy and peace
units.note: overflowing with hope by the power of the Spirit

verses.text: Now may the God of {{elpis|hope}} fill you with all joy and peace as you believe in Him, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.

bastazo.gloss: To carry, to bear a weight, to take up and support. It is more than tolerating; it is lifting and carrying the burden of another's weakness as one's own. The strong are called not to shrug at the failings of the weak but to shoulder them, in the pattern of the Christ who bore our burdens and did not please Himself.

oikodome.gloss: Building up, edification, the construction of a house. Paul uses this image for the growth of the church and of each believer. To please one's neighbor for his good means to act so as to build him up, laying stone upon stone in his faith, rather than tearing down the work of God for the sake of one's own preference.

doxazo.gloss: To glorify, to give glory, to honor and praise. The goal of Christ's coming to Jew and Gentile alike is that God be glorified for His mercy. The whole section is oriented to this end: that the church, welcoming one another, would with one voice glorify God, and that the nations would join Israel in praising Him.

elpis.gloss: Hope, confident expectation. Biblical hope is not wishful thinking but the settled assurance of good that God has promised. Paul calls God the God of hope and prays that believers would overflow with hope by the Spirit's power, grounding the church's unity and joy in the certain future secured by the risen Christ, the Root of Jesse in whom the nations hope.

basic.context: Paul finishes the appeal he began in chapter fourteen. Instead of the strong and the weak despising and judging one another over food and days, they are to welcome one another. He raises the bar for the strong: not merely to allow the weak but to bear their failings and seek their good. And he grounds it all in Christ, who did not please Himself but bore reproach for us, and who came as a servant so that both Jews and Gentiles would praise God together.
basic.hermeneutics: Notice how Paul argues: he moves from practical command to the example of Christ to a chain of Old Testament texts, then to a prayer. The cluster of quotations from the Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets shows that God always intended a worldwide people. Read the section as the theological summit of the whole letter's argument, where Jew and Gentile finally sing together to the glory of God.
basic.originalLanguages: The strong are to bastazo, to carry, the failings of the weak, not merely put up with them. The aim is oikodome, building up the neighbor. The great end is that all would doxazo, glorify, God for His mercy. And the closing prayer commits the church to the God of elpis, hope, who fills His people with joy and peace so that they overflow with hope by the Spirit.
basic.typology: The Root of Jesse from Isaiah is fulfilled in Christ, the Davidic King who rises to rule the nations. The promises to the patriarchs find their yes in Him. The reproaches that fell on the righteous sufferer of the Psalms fall on Christ at the cross. The Scriptures written long ago were written to give us hope, and they point beyond themselves to Him.
basic.christ: Christ is both the example and the ground. He did not please Himself but bore the insults meant for God, taking our reproach at the cross. He became a servant to the circumcised to keep God's promises and to open mercy to the Gentiles. He is the Root of Jesse in whom the nations hope. Because Christ has welcomed us at such cost, we welcome one another to the glory of God.
basic.god: God is the God who gives endurance and encouragement, the God who is glorified when His people live in harmony, and above all the God of hope. His truth and His mercy meet here: He keeps His promises to the patriarchs and He pours out mercy on the nations. The section overflows with His purpose to be praised by a united people from every tongue.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 69 supplies the reproaches that fell on Christ. Isaiah 11 promises the Root of Jesse in whom the Gentiles hope. Deuteronomy 32 and Psalms 18 and 117 call the nations to rejoice with God's people. Romans 15:13 gathers the letter's themes of faith, joy, peace, and hope.
basic.oneStory: From Abraham God promised to bless all nations, and through David He promised a King. Israel's Scriptures kept calling the nations to praise. Now in Christ, the servant of the circumcised and the Root of Jesse, the promise lands: Jew and Gentile welcome one another and glorify God together, overflowing with hope by the Spirit, a foretaste of the countless throng that will praise Him forever.

context.literary:
Romans 15:1 to 13 is the last third of a single argument that began in 14:1, and it works as a landing strip. The earlier verses were mostly addressed to both camps. Here Paul turns to the confident with a first person plural, 'we who are strong', and then does something he rarely does in this letter: he builds a whole paragraph out of Old Testament quotations. Verses 1 to 6 hold the appeal and its grounding in Christ, wrapped by a prayer. Verses 7 to 12 hold the appeal again, now argued from Scripture. Verse 13 is a second prayer. The section is therefore bracketed by two wishes addressed to God, 15:5 and 15:13, each beginning 'Now may the God of'.

The shape inside verses 9 to 12 is careful. Paul sets four quotations in a row, and the introductions climb: 'as it is written', 'again it says', 'and again', 'and once more, Isaiah says'. The sources are drawn from every part of the Hebrew Bible as his readers knew it. Deuteronomy supplies the Law, Psalm 18 and Psalm 117 supply the Writings, and Isaiah supplies the Prophets. The common word in all four is 'Gentiles' or 'peoples'. He is not collecting scattered proof texts. He is showing that the whole canon sings the same line.

The passage is also a deliberate echo of the letter's beginning. Romans 1:16 declared the gospel to the Jew first and also to the Greek, and 1:5 spoke of calling the Gentiles to the obedience of faith. Here those two threads are tied together and the church that has been told to welcome is told why: so that the nations might praise. The doctrinal letter ends its argument on a note of worship, and the benediction of verse 13 is almost a summary of the whole book in a sentence.
context.historical:
The Gentile and Jewish believers in Rome had a history of friction that went beyond food. Jews had been expelled from the city under Claudius, Acts 18:2, and some had returned to find Gentiles leading the church. In a city where Jews were a minority often viewed with suspicion, and where Gentile believers had come to Christ without the long Jewish memory, mutual condescension was easy. Paul's claim in 15:8 and 9 speaks to both sides at once. The Jewish believer is told that Christ came as a servant to his people to keep promises, so he has no reason for bitterness. The Gentile believer is told that his place in the family rests entirely on mercy, not on any right.

The Old Testament texts Paul uses would have been familiar to a synagogue-trained ear. Psalm 18 is David's song of deliverance, in which a king who has conquered his enemies vows to praise the LORD among the nations. Psalm 117 is the shortest psalm in the Psalter, a two verse summons to the nations, sung at Passover as part of the Hallel. Deuteronomy 32 is Moses' great song that ends with the nations rejoicing with God's people. Isaiah 11 belongs to the oracle about the shoot from the stump of Jesse, the Davidic king whose reign will bring peace. Roman believers who knew these passages would have heard them read aloud in worship, and Paul's selection tells them that their own gathering is the fulfilment of what was sung.

There is also a political overtone worth noticing. Rome's emperors were hailed as saviours and lords whose rule would bring peace to the world. Paul's quotation of Isaiah 11:10, 'One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles', puts a rival king before a congregation living in the capital. The hope of the nations does not rest on Caesar but on the Root of Jesse.
context.canonical:
Verse 3 quotes Psalm 69:9, 'The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me'. The same psalm is taken up in John 2:17, where the disciples remember 'Zeal for Your house will consume Me' as Jesus clears the temple, and again in John 15:25 and Romans 11:9 and 10. Psalm 69 was thus read in the early church as the voice of the righteous sufferer, and Paul uses it here to show that Christ bore reproach for the sake of others.

The four quotations of verses 9 to 12 draw on the whole canon, and each has a home. Psalm 18:49 closes David's song, and Paul hears in it a king giving praise among the nations. Deuteronomy 32:43 sits at the end of Moses' witness against Israel, where even a story of failure ends with the nations rejoicing. Psalm 117:1 is a one line summons. Isaiah 11:10 belongs to the section where the Spirit rests on the coming king, Isaiah 11:2.

Verse 4 gives Paul's own rule for reading: what was written in the past was written 'for our instruction'. It sits beside 1 Corinthians 10:11, 2 Timothy 3:16 and 17, and Romans 4:23 and 24. It tells the church that the Old Testament is not a museum piece but a living word that gives hope.

The doctrine of the 'servant of the circumcised' connects to Matthew 15:24 and Mark 10:45, and to the Servant Songs of Isaiah, where the servant brings light to the nations, Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6. The collection of 15:25 to 27 is a visible sign that the blessing promised to Abraham in Genesis 12:3 has reached the nations.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants the strong to carry something, not merely tolerate it. The verb he chose has the sense of lifting a load, and the load is the weak person's scruples, hesitations and immature habits. He then widens the call. The reason is not that the weak are pitiable but that Christ is the pattern. 'Even Christ did not please Himself', 15:3, is the sentence the whole passage turns on. A Gentile Christian with a fine theology of freedom has a model to follow in a Lord who gave up what He was entitled to.

He also wants the church to be a worshipping people rather than a debating society. The aim clause of verse 6 is 'that with one mind and one voice you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ'. The goal of agreement is praise. A congregation that is never of one voice has little to sing about together. By running the Old Testament quotations through the middle of the section, he tells the Romans that their unity is not an experiment but the long-promised event of Jews and Gentiles singing together.

He wants them to hope. Verse 4 and verse 13 frame the section with that word. Believers who put up with one another's weakness will need endurance, and Scripture, Paul says, is God's means of supplying it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the passage is prescription. 'We who are strong ought to bear with the shortcomings of the weak', 15:1, and 'Accept one another', 15:7, are commands. The verbs are plural, so they are directed at the church as a body and not only at individuals. A congregation obeys them by how it welcomes newcomers, how its leaders speak about people who differ, and how its stronger members use their influence.

The description in the passage is of Christ, and it works as a pattern rather than a rule. The example of verse 3 does not mean that every believer must take on the same kind of suffering. It means that the way Christ carries others sets the direction for how we treat one another. The quotation of Psalm 69:9 describes what Christ endured for God's sake, and the church is invited to see itself as the beneficiary of that endurance before it is asked to imitate it.

The four Old Testament quotations are also best read as description. Paul does not say that every Gentile must sing in a Jewish synagogue. He shows that the prophets expected the nations to join the praise of Israel's God, and that expectation is now being met. The proper application is to rejoice in it and to let it shape how a mixed congregation thinks about itself.

debates.question: Who is speaking in Psalm 69:9, as quoted in verse 3?

views.label: Christ speaks through the psalmist
views.case: Many in the church's history have read Psalm 69 as the voice of the Messiah, since the New Testament takes it up repeatedly. John 2:17 applies verse 9 to Jesus, and Paul here says outright that the words 'have fallen on Me' are Christ's. On this reading the Spirit who inspired David's words was also speaking for the one David foreshadowed.

views.label: David speaks as a righteous sufferer, and Christ fulfils the pattern
views.case: Others note that Psalm 69 also contains an admission of folly and guilt before God, Psalm 69:5, which cannot be spoken by Christ. They read the psalm as the prayer of a righteous Israelite who suffers for God's sake, and they see the New Testament use as typological: the pattern of the righteous man who takes the reproach meant for God is fulfilled completely in Jesus.

debates.bearing: On either reading Paul's point holds. The reproach aimed at God fell on Christ, and the body that now bears His name should bear one another.

debates.question: What does Paul mean that Christ is a servant of the circumcised?

views.label: Christ's earthly ministry to Israel confirms the promises
views.case: The phrase points to Jesus' ministry to Jews, as in Matthew 15:24, which makes the saying a historical reminder that the Messiah was first sent to Israel. Verse 8 gives the purpose: to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs, a promise to Abraham that included the nations, Genesis 12:3.

views.label: The phrase is a summary of Christ's whole work for Israel, including the cross
views.case: Others take the perfect tense, 'has become', to include His continuing role as the Davidic King and His death, which fulfilled the covenant. The service is not only a stage in His life but the basis on which Gentiles share in blessings.

debates.bearing: Both views make the same point: the Gentiles come into blessing through Israel's Messiah, so Gentile pride in the church would deny its own foundation, and Jewish pride would deny the purpose of the promise.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 puts the opposition in a striking way. The strong are the dunatoi, the able, and the people they are to bear with are the adunatoi, the unable, whose failings the Greek calls asthenemata. The same family of words has been running through chapter 14, and here the strong are told that they 'ought', opheilomen, a verb of debt. What they owe is not a favour but a payment. The same idea of debt returns in 15:27, where the Gentiles 'owe' it to Jerusalem to share material blessings.

In verse 3 the phrase 'did not please Himself' uses areskein, the verb for pleasing or satisfying. In verse 1 Paul says 'not to please ourselves' with the same verb and in verse 2 'please his neighbour' as well. Paul is not telling anyone to flatter. He is saying that the target of our pleasing has to move away from the self. He adds 'for his good', so that the pleasing is directed to what truly helps.

Verse 4 gives two pairs of nouns that return in verse 5. Endurance, hypomone, and encouragement, paraklesis, are what the Scriptures supply, and in verse 5 they are said to be what God gives. The Bible is thus the instrument and God the giver. The verb in verse 4, 'was written', has a prefix that makes it 'written beforehand'. The earlier Scriptures were written with the present church in view.

The prayer of verse 5 asks God to grant 'harmony'. The Greek is to auto phronein, literally to think the same thing. It is a way of setting the mind, not a call to identical opinions, since chapter 14 has just allowed different convictions about food. The phrase 'in accord with Christ Jesus' that follows gives the standard by which minds are tuned. In verse 6 'with one mind and one voice' joins homothymadon, a word that elsewhere describes the early believers praying together, Acts 1:14, with the picture of a single mouth. The believers are asked to sound like one choir.

In verse 8 the word for 'servant' is diakonos, the very word Paul uses of Phoebe in 16:1. Christ is called a diakonos of the circumcised, which gives the office of service a Christlike pedigree. The next phrase, to confirm the promises, uses a verb of making firm, the language of legal guarantee. The promises were not wobbling, and in Christ they are validated.

Verse 13 is built on two verbs of abundance. The God of hope is asked to fill, pleroo, believers with joy and peace, so that they 'overflow', perisseuo, with hope. The two words are related, since one speaks of the container filled and the other of the container spilling over. The little phrase 'as you believe', literally in the believing, makes faith the channel through which the filling arrives.

typology.fulfillment: Isaiah pictures a shoot from the stump of Jesse, a king on whom the Spirit rests, and then says the root of Jesse will 'stand as a banner for the peoples' so that 'the nations will seek Him', Isaiah 11:1, 2 and 10. Paul uses the Greek form, in which the king 'will arise to rule over the Gentiles'. In Christ the pattern becomes a person: Revelation 22:16 has Jesus say 'I am the Root and the Offspring of David'. The correspondence is that a Davidic king rules the nations, and the escalation is that the kingdom He establishes is not Israel's borders but all peoples, with hope placed in Him personally. The type falls short in that David's house produced many kings who failed, while this King does not.

The psalmist bears shame, estrangement from his own family and the insults of God's enemies, Psalm 69:7 to 9. The pattern is that the person closest to God's honour takes the blows meant for God. Jesus is the one in whom it is completed. John 2:17 uses the same psalm of His zeal for the temple, and Romans 15:3 uses it of the reproach He took. The escalation is that His suffering is not only a witness against the world but a bearing of the load of others, Isaiah 53:4. The type falls short because the psalmist also confesses his own guilt, Psalm 69:5, while Christ bore the reproach with none of His own.

typology.type: The promises to the patriarchs confirmed
typology.fulfillment: God's word to Abraham, 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you', Genesis 12:3, was repeated to Isaac and Jacob. These promises were like a mortgage drawn on a future that Israel could see only from far off, Hebrews 11:13. Paul says Christ has become the servant who 'confirms' them, 15:8, and Luke 1:54 and 55 had already framed His coming as God remembering mercy to Abraham. The correspondence is complete in that every promise finds its yes in Him, 2 Corinthians 1:20. The pattern is not yet closed, since the full gathering of the nations is still described as a future multitude, Revelation 7:9.

typology.type: The Gentiles' song among the nations
typology.fulfillment: David's vow in Psalm 18:49 to praise God among the nations was spoken by a king in Israel to whom the nations were mostly enemies. Its pattern was that of the praise of Israel's God crossing the border. In Paul's day the vow is being carried out by a mixed congregation of Jews and Gentiles singing together. The escalation is that those who were once outside now sing as insiders, and the song is led by the Root of Jesse. The type falls short only in being unfinished, since the praise of every tongue, Philippians 2:11, remains ahead.

study.christ:
Christ appears in this passage as the pattern, the servant, the promise and the hope of the nations, and Paul gives each a text.

The pattern comes first. 'Even Christ did not please Himself', verse 3. The word 'even' is bold. If anyone could have insisted on his rights, it was the Son of God. Philippians 2:3 to 8 describes the same self-emptying, and Luke 22:27 records His own claim: 'I am among you as one who serves'. Paul asks the strong believer to see himself as someone with something to give up, and the Lord with the greatest rights is the one who gave them up first. Paul quotes Psalm 69:9, in which the reproaches aimed at God land on the speaker. The words are placed on Christ's lips. In the cross, the insults that humanity hurled at God fell on the Son, and He carried them. The sentence is not primarily about sin. It is about how far Christ went to take on the cost of another's offence.

Then the servant. Verse 8 says Christ 'has become a servant of the circumcised on behalf of God's truth, to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs'. God's truth is His faithfulness to what He said. Christ is how God's word to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob is made good. The same sentence continues, 'so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy', which links truth to mercy. God keeps His promise to Israel in a way that opens mercy to the nations, and the two aims are one act. Mark 10:45 says the Son of Man came 'to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many', and Romans 15:8 shows the same service seen from the side of the promise.

Then the promise. Galatians 3:16 says the promises to Abraham were made to his offspring, who is Christ, and Romans 15:12 uses Isaiah to say that this offspring will rule. Isaiah 11:2 ties the Davidic king to the Spirit's rest on Him, which Paul echoes in verse 13, where believers overflow with hope by the power of the Spirit. The king who bears the Spirit is the giver of the Spirit.

Finally, the hope of the nations. 'In Him the Gentiles will put their hope.' The sentence is built on Christ as the object of hope. Believers who once had no hope and were without God in the world, Ephesians 2:12, now rest it on a person. Everything in the passage that tells the strong to bear the weak depends on that. They are not asked to produce unity out of their own resources. They are asked to look at the one in whom the whole family has been gathered.

A caution: not every Old Testament phrase in the catena is a prediction of a single event. Paul is gathering Scriptures that show God's purpose and applying them to the work of Christ and the church. The links stand because the New Testament makes them, not because we can find a hidden Jesus behind every verse of the Psalms.
study.god:
The God of this passage has several names in a few verses, and each says something. He is 'the God who gives endurance and encouragement', 15:5. He is 'the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ', 15:6. He is the God of truth and of mercy, 15:8 and 9. He is 'the God of hope', 15:13. Each name belongs to the people He is addressing. The church needs endurance because the work of bearing others is long, and it needs encouragement because the work wears people out. It needs to know the Father because Christ's example makes sense only inside a family. It needs the God of truth and mercy because the Jew needs reassurance that promises are kept and the Gentile needs reassurance that grace is real. And it needs the God of hope to overflow rather than to scrape by.

He is a God whose truth and mercy do not compete. Verses 8 and 9 line them up: Christ confirms the promises 'on behalf of God's truth', so that Gentiles may glorify Him 'for His mercy'. A tidy theology might say that truth is for the Jews and mercy for the Gentiles. Paul says both are for everyone. God's fidelity to Israel is the means by which His mercy reaches the nations. Because He kept His word to Abraham, the nations can trust Him.

He is a God who speaks through Scripture to shape character. Verse 4 does not say that the Old Testament teaches us facts. It says that through endurance and encouragement we might have hope. God uses His written word as a tool to produce a settled, hopeful life, and He is also the one who gives the endurance, 15:5. The Scriptures are His instrument, and the Spirit is His power, 15:13.

He is a God who delights in being praised by many voices. The word 'glorify' runs through the section, 15:6, 7 and 9, and every quotation is a call to praise. God's purpose for His church is not private contentment but a chorus that includes people from different places and histories. A congregation that fails to welcome those God has welcomed loses part of the praise He is owed.

He is a God who fills. Verse 13 does not ask Him for a little more hope. It asks Him to fill believers with all joy and peace, and to let them overflow. The generous scale matches His character as the God of hope, whose supply is not measured by what the church can already see.

For worship, the passage offers a model in the prayers of verses 5 and 13. Paul prays for what he commands. He tells the Romans to welcome one another and asks God to make it possible. That honesty is a pattern for congregations: obedience to such commands begins with asking for the grace to keep them.

crossReferences.note: The psalmist bears scorn for God's sake and is estranged from his own family because zeal for God's house consumed him. Paul quotes the end of verse 9 and gives it to Christ. Reading the whole verse shows how closely the sufferer's loyalty to God's honour matches Christ's own.

The disciples remember Psalm 69:9 when Jesus clears the temple. It shows that the same psalm which Paul uses of Christ's bearing reproach was understood by His first followers as His own words, so the link in Romans 15:3 was not invented by Paul.

Paul urges believers to count others better than themselves and describes how Christ, though in the form of God, took the form of a servant and became obedient to death. It is the same argument as Romans 15:1 to 3, set out in a hymn and showing why the strong should give way.

Believers are told to carry one another's burdens and so fulfil the law of Christ, using the same verb of bearing as in Romans 15:1. It gives the commanded action a name and shows that burden bearing is Christ's own law and not an optional kindness.

All the families of the earth are to be blessed through Abraham. Paul's claim in Romans 15:8 and 9 that Christ confirms the promises to the patriarchs so that Gentiles glorify God for mercy is the point at which this old promise finally arrives.

David vows to praise the LORD among the nations and sing to His name. Paul puts the vow in the mouth of Christ among the Gentiles, as the first of four quotations showing that the nations were always meant to join Israel's praise.

At the end of Moses' song the nations are summoned to rejoice with God's people. It is striking that a song of rebuke to Israel ends in the nations' joy. Paul takes it as the Law's own witness to a worldwide family.

The shortest psalm in the Psalter calls all nations and all peoples to praise the LORD. Paul uses it as the third voice in his chorus. It shows that Gentile praise is not an afterthought but a call as ancient as Israel's songbook.

A shoot from Jesse's stump, anointed with the Spirit, will judge in righteousness and stand as a banner for the peoples. Paul quotes only verse 10, but the whole oracle explains why the nations will hope in Him: He rules by justice and peace.

All of God's promises find their yes in Christ. It gives the doctrinal basis for Romans 15:8, where Christ confirms the promises, and shows that the work is not only a Jewish matter but the central confirmation of everything God has said.

Everything written in the past was written for our instruction, that through endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. It sits next to 1 Corinthians 10:11 and 2 Timothy 3:16 and 17 as Paul's own guide to reading the Old Testament.

Gentiles once far off are brought near through the blood of Christ, and the dividing wall of hostility between them and Israel is broken down. It describes the reality that Romans 15 commands the church to live out, one new humanity in place of two.

study.oneStory:
The scene of Romans 15 is a congregation, but the story it belongs to runs from Genesis to Revelation. God's first word to Abraham already had the nations in view: 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you', Genesis 12:3. The rest of the Old Testament keeps that promise alive in unexpected places. Moses' last song ends with the nations rejoicing, Deuteronomy 32:43. David vows to praise God among them, Psalm 18:49. A two verse psalm calls them to extol Him, Psalm 117:1. Isaiah sees a king who will stand as a banner for them, Isaiah 11:10. What looks in the pages of the Law and the Prophets like a thread of hope pulling against the weight of Israel's failures turns out to be the main line.

By the time Paul writes, the thread has become a rope. In Christ the promises to the patriarchs are confirmed, the nations have begun to come in, and Jewish and Gentile believers are meeting in the same rooms. The first test of that new situation is not a great persecution but a quarrel over what to eat and which days to keep. Paul's answer shows that the story of redemption is also the story of how redeemed people treat one another. The church lives out the one story by welcoming the person who is different.

Seen against the whole plan, the verb 'accept' in verse 7 has a long history. Genesis 3 ended with a man and woman sent out from God's presence, hiding from one another and from Him. Each part of the story since then has been about God taking people back and making them welcome. Christ's acceptance is the climax of it. When a church makes room for the awkward, the slow and the scrupulous, it is repeating in miniature what God has done for them.

The story ends where verse 13 points, with joy and peace overflowing in a hope that is no longer anxious. Revelation 7:9 shows the destination: a multitude from every nation and tribe and people and tongue standing before the throne, all singing the same song. They are not asked to give up their languages or histories. They are asked to praise the same Lamb. Romans 15 is a rehearsal for that day, and every congregation that learns to sing in harmony over its differences is practising it.

quiz.q: What are the strong called to do for the weak in verses 1 and 2?

options.text: Bear with their shortcomings and please them for their good, to build them up.
options.note: The strong are to carry the weak and seek their edification, not their own pleasure.

options.text: Tolerate them while quietly pleasing themselves.
options.note: Bearing with the weak is right, but Paul says not to please ourselves; the aim is their good and their upbuilding.

options.text: Leave them alone to work out their own faith.
options.note: Paul calls for active bearing and building up, not detachment.

options.text: Insist they abandon their scruples immediately.
options.note: The command is to bear with them, not to demand they change at once.

quiz.q: What example does Paul give to ground this call?

options.text: Christ did not please Himself but bore the reproaches meant for God.
options.note: Paul cites Psalm 69 to point to Christ's self-giving as the pattern.

options.text: The example of the Old Testament kings.
options.note: Paul points to Christ, the Root of Jesse, not to the kings as models here.

options.text: His own personal sacrifices as an apostle.
options.note: Paul does model self-giving, but the example he grounds this in is Christ, who did not please Himself.

options.text: The Roman believers' past record of unity.
options.note: The example is Christ who did not please Himself.

quiz.q: According to verses 8 and 9, why did Christ become a servant of the circumcised?

options.text: To confirm the promises to the patriarchs and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy.
options.note: Christ keeps the promises to Israel and opens mercy to the nations.

options.text: To replace Israel entirely with the Gentile church.
options.note: Paul grounds Gentile praise in Israel's Scriptures, not in displacing Israel.

options.text: To abolish God's promises to the patriarchs.
options.note: Christ came to confirm those promises, not abolish them.

options.text: To serve only the Jewish people and no others.
options.note: Christ did serve the circumcised to confirm the promises, but the goal reaches further, that the Gentiles too might glorify God for His mercy.

quiz.q: Why does Paul chain together four Old Testament quotations in verses 9 to 12?

options.text: To show from Scripture that God always purposed Jew and Gentile to praise Him together.
options.note: The Law, Psalms, and Prophets all foretell the nations praising God.

options.text: To prove that the Old Testament is no longer relevant.
options.note: Paul treats the Scriptures as authoritative and fulfilled, not obsolete.

options.text: To settle a dispute about which foods are clean.
options.note: The wider context concerns the weak and the strong over food, but here the quotations aim to show Jew and Gentile praising God together.

options.text: To display his skill at quoting texts.
options.note: The purpose is theological, to ground Gentile inclusion in Scripture.

quiz.q: What does Paul pray for in the benediction of verse 13?

options.text: That the God of hope would fill them with joy and peace so they overflow with hope by the Spirit.
options.note: The blessing gathers joy, peace, and overflowing hope by the Spirit's power.

options.text: That they would gain worldly success and comfort.
options.note: The prayer is for joy, peace, and hope in God, not worldly gain.

options.text: That they would simply feel more optimistic.
options.note: Paul prays for real joy, peace, and overflowing hope by the Spirit, which is far more than mere optimism.

options.text: That they would be freed from all future suffering.
options.note: The hope is by the Spirit amid life, not a promise of no suffering now.

questions: Paul calls the strong not merely to tolerate the weak but to bear their failings, as Christ bore ours. Whose burden is God asking you to shoulder rather than shrug off?
Christ did not please Himself but took the reproaches meant for God. Where is God calling you to lay down your own comfort or preference for the good of another believer?
We are to welcome one another just as Christ welcomed us. How does the cost and warmth of Christ's welcome of you change the way you receive people you find difficult?
Paul shows from Scripture that God always planned to gather every nation to praise Him. How does belonging to that worldwide, promised people shape your view of your local church?

The God of hope wants to fill you with joy and peace so that you overflow with hope by the Spirit. Where do you most need that overflowing hope right now, and how might you seek it in believing prayer?

translationNotes.note: The quotation is from Psalm 69:9, a psalm of the suffering righteous one; Paul applies the reproaches that fell on the psalmist to Christ, who bore the insults meant for God.
Paul strings together Psalm 18:49 with 2 Samuel 22:50, then Deuteronomy 32:43 and Psalm 117:1, drawing from the Law, the Writings, and the Prophets to show the nations praising God with Israel.
The Root of Jesse is from Isaiah 11:10; the wording follows the Greek Old Testament, which speaks of the nations hoping in Him, fulfilled in the risen Christ, the Davidic King over the Gentiles.
